nameStory: Yarrow gets its name from the Old English 'gearwe,' meaning 'to prepare' or 'to make ready' - a nod to its long history as a healing herb. Legend says the Greek hero Achilles used yarrow to treat his soldiers' wounds during the Trojan War, which is why its scientific name is Achillea. The 'millefolium' part means 'thousand leaves,' describing its delicately divided, feathery foliage.
description: Common yarrow is a hardy perennial wildflower that grows up to 3 feet tall with distinctive flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers. Its most recognizable feature is its soft, feathery leaves that look almost like green lace or fern fronds. The entire plant has a strong, somewhat medicinal smell when crushed. You'll often see it growing in patches along roadsides, in fields, and even pushing up through cracks in sidewalks.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Feathery, fern-like leaves that are finely divided into countless tiny segments, feeling soft and almost fluffy to the touch. They alternate up the stem and release a strong, pungent herbal scent when crushed.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers (occasionally pink) that form a landing pad about 2-4 inches across. Each tiny flower head looks like a miniature daisy with 4-6 white petals around a yellowish center.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows 1-3 feet tall with sturdy, upright stems that may have a slightly fuzzy texture. Often forms colonies through underground runners, creating patches of multiple plants.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, flattened seeds with tiny wings that develop in late summer, turning the flower heads brown and papery. The dried seed heads often persist into winter.

habitat: Yarrow thrives in sunny, open areas with well-drained soil throughout New England. You'll find it in old fields, meadows, roadsides, waste places, and even poor, rocky soils where other plants struggle. It's particularly common in disturbed areas and seems to love spots that get mowed occasionally but not constantly.

seasonality.spring: New feathery leaves emerge early, forming low rosettes. The distinctive lacy foliage is already identifiable by late spring even before flowers appear.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season from June through August, when the characteristic flat-topped white flower clusters are most prominent and fragrant.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade to brown seed heads, and leaves may turn yellowish. Seeds disperse in early fall, but some dried flower heads persist.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, but dried stems and seed heads may remain standing. Look for old basal leaves near the ground in mild periods.

funFact: Yarrow is one of nature's most accurate weather predictors - folklore says if you can smell its pungent aroma from several feet away without crushing it, rain is coming within 24 hours because the plant releases more oils in humid air!
confusionNotes: Wild carrot (Queen Anne's lace) also has white flower clusters, but yarrow's flowers form flat tops while Queen Anne's lace makes bird's-nest shaped cups. Remember: yarrow has feathery leaves like ferns, while wild carrot has divided leaves more like actual carrot tops.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its reputation as a healing herb, yarrow can cause skin irritation in sensitive people and should never be consumed without expert guidance. The plant contains compounds that can be toxic in large quantities, so admire its beauty and toughness but don't use it medicinally without proper knowledge.
compareHints: Common yarrow differs from sneezewort (its closest New England relative) by having finely divided, feathery leaves instead of simple, lance-shaped leaves. Fern-leaf yarrow, occasionally found in gardens, has even more finely divided leaves and bright yellow flowers rather than white. Common yarrow is by far the most widespread species you'll encounter in the wild.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its relative common yarrow with deeply divided, feathery leaves, sneezewort has simple, narrow leaves with toothed edges.
Fern-leaf yarrow stands out from its relatives by being the tallest yarrow species and having the most intensely golden-yellow flowers.
Boreal yarrow is nearly identical to common yarrow in appearance - both have the same feathery leaves and white flower clusters.
